papers.title: Post-Training Shifts Confidence: A Three-Stage Analysis of How SFT, RL, and OPD Shape Pre-, Intra-, and Post-CoT Calibration
papers.abstract: Large language models have made strong reasoning gains through supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, and on-policy distillation, yet these post-training methods are usually evaluated only by final-answer accuracy. We study how they reshape confidence during reasoning. We introduce a three-stage calibration framework that evaluates confidence before, during, and after chain-of-thought generation, corresponding to difficulty estimation, early termination, and answer aggregation. Through a controlled comparison on mathematical reasoning benchmarks, we find that OPD provides the most useful pre-reasoning confidence, SFT gives the strongest online signal for early stopping, and RL produces the most reliable trace-level signal for aggregation. We further show that confidence reliability is position-dependent: RL confidence becomes informative after a path-commitment phase, while OPD confidence is useful early but can become inversely calibrated later. Based on this observation, we propose PosConf, a position-aware confidence strategy that uses confidence only from reliable relative-position intervals. PosConf improves RL answer aggregation by 6.1 points over majority voting and consistently improves OPD early stopping under tight token budgets, with gains up to 4.3 points by avoiding its later inverse-calibration region, showing that \emph{confidence in reasoning models should be used both stage-wise and position-awarely}. Our code is available at https://github.com/EIT-NLP/Post-Training-Calibration.

summary.takeaway: Reasoning-oriented post-training methods (SFT, RL, OPD) induce distinct, stage-dependent shifts in confidence calibration, which can be leveraged position-awarely to improve reasoning efficiency and accuracy.
summary.problem: Existing evaluations of post-training methods focus on final-answer accuracy, neglecting how these methods reshape confidence calibration before, during, and after chain-of-thought reasoning.
summary.method: The paper introduces a three-stage confidence calibration framework (Pre-CoT, Intra-CoT, Post-CoT) to systematically analyze and compare how SFT, RL, and OPD affect confidence signals at different reasoning stages and positions.
summary.evidence: Controlled experiments on mathematical reasoning benchmarks with Qwen2.5-7B variants show OPD excels at pre-reasoning difficulty estimation, SFT provides the strongest intra-reasoning early stopping signal, and RL yields the most reliable post-reasoning aggregation confidence, with PosConf improving RL aggregation by 6.1 points and OPD early stopping by up to 4.3 points.
summary.limitations: The study is limited to a single backbone (Qwen2.5-7B) and mathematical reasoning benchmarks, with no evidence on other model families, domains, or downstream tasks.
summary.why_for_you: Understanding how post-training paradigms reshape confidence calibration stage-wise and position-awarely enables designing more trustworthy and efficient LLM reasoning systems through improved uncertainty estimation and inference-time decisions.

signals.text: OPD provides the most informative Pre-CoT confidence for problem difficulty estimation, achieving the highest AUROC and PRR scores across multiple mathematical benchmarks.

The PosConf strategy uses position-aware confidence intervals to selectively leverage reliable confidence signals, improving RL answer aggregation by 6.1 points over majority voting and enhancing OPD early stopping under tight token budgets.

Confidence reliability is position-dependent: RL confidence becomes informative only after a path-commitment phase, while OPD confidence is useful early but can become inversely calibrated later in the reasoning trace.

deep_dive.overview: This paper addresses the gap in understanding how different post-training methods—supervised fine-tuning (SFT), reinforcement learning (RL), and on-policy distillation (OPD)—reshape confidence calibration in large language models during chain-of-thought reasoning. Instead of treating confidence as a monolithic final output property, the authors propose a three-stage framework evaluating confidence before reasoning (Pre-CoT), during reasoning (Intra-CoT), and after reasoning (Post-CoT). Using Qwen2.5-7B-based models trained on the same data but with different post-training objectives, they conduct controlled experiments on diverse mathematical reasoning benchmarks. Results show that OPD excels at pre-reasoning difficulty estimation, SFT provides the strongest online signal for early termination of low-quality reasoning traces, and RL yields the most reliable confidence for answer aggregation. They further reveal that confidence calibration varies with token position, motivating PosConf, a position-aware confidence strategy that selectively uses confidence from reliable relative-position intervals. PosConf significantly improves RL aggregation accuracy and OPD early stopping efficiency, demonstrating that confidence should be used both stage-wise and position-awarely to enhance reasoning reliability and efficiency.

methodology.title: Three-Stage Confidence Calibration Framework
methodology.detail: The framework partitions confidence evaluation into Pre-CoT (before chain-of-thought generation, assessing problem difficulty), Intra-CoT (during generation, enabling early termination of uncertain traces), and Post-CoT (after generation, supporting answer aggregation). Confidence is computed from top-k next-token probabilities, smoothed over sliding windows, and normalized by relative token position.

methodology.title: Model Variants and Training
methodology.detail: Four Qwen2.5-7B-based models are compared: Qwen-Instruct (instruction-tuned baseline), Qwen-SFT (supervised fine-tuned on correct chain-of-thought traces), Qwen-RL (trained with group relative policy optimization using binary outcome rewards), and Qwen-OPD (on-policy distillation from a larger teacher model via dense KL divergence). All models share the same backbone and training data to isolate post-training effects.

methodology.title: Confidence Metrics and Evaluation
methodology.detail: Pre-CoT confidence is evaluated by AUROC and PRR to measure difficulty prediction quality. Intra-CoT confidence triggers early stopping when sliding window confidence falls below a threshold, balancing token usage and accuracy. Post-CoT confidence ranks completed traces for confidence-filtered majority voting and most-confident selection, assessing aggregation improvements.

methodology.title: PosConf Position-Aware Confidence Strategy
methodology.detail: PosConf restricts confidence usage to reliable relative-position intervals identified by analyzing confidence calibration dynamics across token positions. This avoids inverse calibration regions, improving early stopping and answer aggregation by leveraging only trustworthy confidence segments.

mechanism.title: Token-Level Confidence Computation
mechanism.detail: Confidence at token position ℓ is computed as the negative average log probability over the top-k next-token candidates, smoothed over a sliding window of size w to capture local uncertainty dynamics. Relative token position ρt = t/m normalizes positions across traces of varying lengths, enabling position-aware confidence analysis.

mechanism.title: No Explicit Theoretical Mechanism Provided
mechanism.detail: The paper does not provide formal equations or causal theories beyond the confidence computation formula and the empirical observation of position-dependent calibration shifts.

experiments.title: Pre-CoT Difficulty Estimation
experiments.detail: Evaluated on mathematical reasoning benchmarks (AIME 24/25, AMC 23, MATH500) using AUROC and PRR metrics, comparing Qwen-Instruct, Qwen-SFT, Qwen-RL, and Qwen-OPD. OPD achieves the highest average AUROC (0.644) and PRR (0.345), indicating superior pre-reasoning confidence calibration.

experiments.title: Intra-CoT Early Stopping
experiments.detail: Confidence thresholds are swept to produce token-accuracy frontiers under a fixed budget of 256 traces per problem. Early stopping triggered when sliding window confidence falls below threshold reduces token usage without accuracy loss. SFT yields the strongest online signal for early termination.

experiments.title: Post-CoT Answer Aggregation
experiments.detail: Answer aggregation compares majority voting, confidence-filtered majority voting (top 5% or 10% traces by confidence), and most-confident selection. RL confidence filtering improves aggregation accuracy by 6.1 points over majority voting, demonstrating reliable trace-level confidence.

experiments.title: PosConf Evaluation
experiments.detail: PosConf applies position-aware confidence intervals to improve RL aggregation and OPD early stopping. It avoids later inverse-calibration regions in OPD, yielding up to 4.3 points gain under tight token budgets.

findings.title: OPD Excels at Pre-CoT Confidence
findings.detail: OPD achieves the highest AUROC and PRR scores for difficulty estimation across multiple benchmarks, outperforming SFT, RL, and the baseline Qwen-Instruct, indicating its pre-reasoning confidence is most informative.

findings.title: SFT Provides Strongest Intra-CoT Signal
findings.detail: During reasoning, SFT yields the most reliable token-level confidence for early stopping, enabling efficient pruning of low-quality reasoning traces without compromising accuracy.

findings.title: RL Confidence Best for Post-CoT Aggregation
findings.detail: RL produces the most reliable trace-level confidence for answer aggregation, improving accuracy by 6.1 points over majority voting when using confidence-filtered voting.

findings.title: Confidence Calibration is Position-Dependent
findings.detail: RL confidence becomes informative only after a path-commitment phase, while OPD confidence is useful early but can become inversely calibrated later, motivating position-aware confidence usage.

findings.title: PosConf Improves Reasoning Efficiency and Accuracy
findings.detail: By restricting confidence usage to reliable relative-position intervals, PosConf improves RL answer aggregation by 6.1 points and OPD early stopping by up to 4.3 points, demonstrating the benefit of stage-wise and position-aware confidence strategies.

contributions: Introduced a three-stage confidence calibration framework (Pre-CoT, Intra-CoT, Post-CoT) linking confidence signals to inference-time decisions in reasoning.
Provided a controlled comparison of SFT, RL, and OPD post-training methods showing distinct stage-dependent confidence calibration shifts.
Discovered position-dependent confidence reliability and proposed PosConf, a position-aware confidence strategy that improves early stopping and answer aggregation.
limitations: Experiments are limited to the Qwen2.5-7B backbone and mathematical reasoning benchmarks, limiting generalizability to other models and tasks.
No evaluation on downstream applications beyond mathematical reasoning or on other types of reasoning tasks.
The study does not explore the impact of varying training data or model architectures on confidence calibration.
No formal theoretical mechanism or causal explanation is provided for the observed position-dependent calibration shifts.
open_questions: How do confidence calibration dynamics generalize across different LLM architectures and larger-scale models?
Can position-aware confidence strategies like PosConf be adapted to other reasoning domains or multimodal tasks?
What are the underlying causes of inverse calibration in OPD confidence at later token positions?
How can confidence calibration be integrated with other uncertainty estimation methods to further improve trustworthy LLM reasoning?

papers.title: Traffic-Aware Randomized Smoothing for LLM-Based Network Intrusion Detection
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based intrusion detection systems (IDS) are increasingly studied for security monitoring, yet their robustness against feasible traffic manipulation remains largely empirical. We present Traffic-Aware Randomized Smoothing (TA-RS), a classifier-agnostic certified defense that injects Gaussian noise exclusively into the directly controllable (DC) subspace -- features a remote attacker can modify -- during both fine-tuning and certification, aligning the smoothing distribution with the attacker-controllable subspace. We identify a critical prerequisite: applying standard randomized smoothing to clean-trained LLM-IDS yields weak certified accuracy in three of four (model, dataset) pairs tested (14-33%, at or below random) and only 57% in the fourth (43 pp below the noise-augmented result); noise-augmented fine-tuning recovers to 68-100% on two of three benchmark datasets (at sigma=0.25). At the L_inf-equivalent threshold R_inf = epsilon*sqrt(|DC|) (epsilon=0.05), TA-RS achieves 55-100% certified accuracy on CIC-IDS-2018 and HIKARI-2021, with median certified radii (R approx 0.45-0.96) exceeding R_inf by 1.8-5x (across sigma=0.25-1.00). Against a fairly trained iso-trained RS baseline the residual advantage is dataset-dependent (4-19 pp on CIC-IDS-2018). The larger gap -- up to 72 pp against an isotropic RS baseline that shares the DC-noise-augmented training recipe -- primarily reflects the training-certification mismatch rather than DC alignment alone: isotropic test-time noise perturbs uncontrollable features the attacker cannot exploit, triggering abstention rates up to 68%. RT-IoT2022 probes the limits of the method: it fails under the default fine-tuning recipe but recovers to 76%/69% certified accuracy (LLaMA3-8B/Qwen3-8B) when noise augmentation is increased.
papers.comment: 44 pages, 14 figures, 14 tables. Submitted to Expert Systems with Applications

summary.takeaway: Traffic-Aware Randomized Smoothing (TA-RS) certifies robustness of LLM-based intrusion detection by injecting Gaussian noise only into attacker-controllable traffic features, achieving 55–100% certified accuracy on key datasets.
summary.problem: LLM-based network intrusion detection systems lack certified robustness guarantees aligned with the feasible attacker-controlled traffic feature subspace.
summary.method: TA-RS injects Gaussian noise exclusively into the directly controllable (DC) feature subspace during both fine-tuning and certification, aligning smoothing with the attacker’s feasible perturbation space.
summary.evidence: TA-RS achieves 55–100% certified accuracy on CIC-IDS-2018 and HIKARI-2021 at ε=0.05, with median certified radii exceeding the L∞ threshold by 1.8–5×, outperforming isotropic randomized smoothing baselines by up to 72 percentage points.
summary.limitations: TA-RS requires dataset-specific noise-augmented fine-tuning for noise stability; it fails under default recipes on challenging datasets like RT-IoT2022 without increased noise augmentation.
summary.why_for_you: TA-RS provides a principled, scalable certified defense framework for LLM-based IDS that aligns certification with realistic attacker capabilities, addressing robustness gaps in adversarial network security.

signals.text: Noise-augmented fine-tuning is critical: clean-trained LLM-IDS yield weak certified accuracy (14–33%), while noise-augmented models recover 68–100% certified accuracy on CIC-IDS-2018 and HIKARI-2021 at σ=0.25.

TA-RS injects Gaussian noise only into the DC subspace (features attacker can modify) during training and certification, avoiding perturbations on indirectly or uncontrollable features that cause high abstention rates (up to 68%) in isotropic smoothing.

Certification radii from TA-RS exceed the L∞-equivalent threshold R∞ by 1.8–5×, demonstrating stronger robustness guarantees; residual advantages over isotropic RS baselines vary by dataset (4–19 pp), mainly due to training-certification distribution mismatch.

deep_dive.overview: This work addresses the robustness of LLM-based network intrusion detection systems (IDS) against adversarial traffic manipulations constrained to attacker-controllable features. The authors formalize a taxonomy partitioning traffic features into directly controllable (DC), indirectly controllable (IC), and uncontrollable (UC) sets, focusing certification on the DC subspace. They propose Traffic-Aware Randomized Smoothing (TA-RS), which injects Gaussian noise exclusively into DC features during both fine-tuning and certification, aligning the smoothing distribution with the feasible attacker perturbation space. Empirical results on three benchmark datasets (CIC-IDS-2018, HIKARI-2021, RT-IoT2022) show that noise-augmented fine-tuning is essential to achieve noise stability and meaningful certified accuracy. TA-RS achieves 55–100% certified accuracy at an L∞-equivalent perturbation budget ε=0.05, with median certified radii exceeding the theoretical threshold by up to 5×. Compared to isotropic randomized smoothing baselines, TA-RS reduces abstention rates drastically and improves certified accuracy by up to 72 percentage points. The method is classifier-agnostic and scalable to billion-parameter LLMs, but requires dataset-specific fine-tuning and increased noise augmentation on challenging datasets. This framework provides a principled, scalable approach to certified robustness in traffic-domain LLM-IDS.

methodology.title: DC/IC/UC Feature Taxonomy
methodology.detail: The authors categorize network traffic features into directly controllable (DC), indirectly controllable (IC), and uncontrollable (UC) sets based on attacker reachability, defining the certification subspace as the DC features that an attacker can realistically perturb.

methodology.title: Noise-Augmented Fine-Tuning
methodology.detail: LLM-based IDS models are fine-tuned with Gaussian noise injected only into DC features to stabilize predictions under noise, enabling effective certification; this step is critical as clean-trained models yield near-random certified accuracy.

methodology.title: Traffic-Aware Randomized Smoothing (TA-RS)
methodology.detail: TA-RS applies Gaussian noise exclusively to the DC subspace during certification, estimating class probabilities via Monte Carlo sampling and computing certified radii using a Neyman–Pearson-based bound adapted to the DC subspace.

methodology.title: Certification Algorithm (TA-Certify)
methodology.detail: TA-Certify draws noise samples restricted to DC features, identifies the top predicted class, estimates a Clopper–Pearson lower confidence bound on its probability, and returns a certified radius or abstains if confidence is insufficient.

methodology.title: Evaluation Metrics and Protocol
methodology.detail: Certified accuracy CA(r) is reported at radius r, penalizing incorrect predictions and abstentions; experiments use fixed train/test splits, protocol-derived feature clipping, and matched noise levels and sample counts for fair comparison with isotropic RS baselines.

mechanism.title: Certified Robustness in DC Subspace
mechanism.detail: The certification guarantee restricts perturbations to the DC subspace, leveraging the injection of Gaussian noise only in this subspace. The Neyman–Pearson lemma applies in the reduced dimension, yielding a certified radius R = σΦ−1(pA) that bounds adversarial perturbations feasible to the attacker. This avoids wasted noise budget and high abstention caused by perturbing uncontrollable features.

experiments.title: Datasets and Setup
experiments.detail: Experiments use three network-traffic datasets: CIC-IDS-2018 (4 classes, 25 features, 14 DC), HIKARI-2021 (3 classes, 82 features, 25 DC), and RT-IoT2022 (5 classes, 83 features, 27 DC). Fixed train/test splits and protocol-derived feature clipping are applied. Certification subsets contain 120–168 samples stratified by class.

experiments.title: Baseline Comparisons
experiments.detail: TA-RS is compared against isotropic randomized smoothing baselines with matched noise levels and training recipes. Certified accuracy and abstention rates are measured at ε=0.05 L∞-equivalent budget, with Monte Carlo sample counts N0=20 and N=200.

experiments.title: Noise-Augmentation Ablation
experiments.detail: Ablations show that noise-augmented fine-tuning is necessary to achieve meaningful certified accuracy; clean-trained LLM-IDS yield 14–33% certified accuracy, while noise-augmented models reach 68–100% on CIC-IDS-2018 and HIKARI-2021.

experiments.title: RT-IoT2022 Challenge
experiments.detail: On the challenging RT-IoT2022 dataset, default fine-tuning fails (≤24% certified accuracy), but increasing noise augmentation recovers 76% (LLaMA3-8B) and 69% (Qwen3-8B) certified accuracy, highlighting noise stability as a key constraint.

findings.title: Certified Accuracy Gains
findings.detail: TA-RS achieves 55–100% certified accuracy on CIC-IDS-2018 and HIKARI-2021 at ε=0.05, with median certified radii 1.8–5× larger than the L∞ threshold, demonstrating strong robustness aligned with attacker capabilities.

findings.title: Abstention Reduction
findings.detail: TA-RS reduces abstention rates drastically compared to isotropic RS (from 68% to 8% on CIC-IDS-2018), by avoiding noise perturbations on uncontrollable features that cause prediction instability.

findings.title: Training-Certification Match Importance
findings.detail: The main advantage of TA-RS over isotropic RS is due to matching noise injection during training and certification, rather than DC subspace selection alone, as isotropic test-time noise perturbs uncontrollable features causing high abstention.

findings.title: Dataset-Dependent Residual Advantage
findings.detail: Against an iso-trained RS baseline, TA-RS shows a residual certified accuracy advantage of 4–19 percentage points on CIC-IDS-2018, indicating dataset-dependent benefits beyond training-certification alignment.

findings.title: Noise Stability as Bottleneck
findings.detail: On RT-IoT2022, TA-RS fails under default fine-tuning but recovers with increased noise augmentation, confirming that noise stability of the base LLM is the binding constraint in challenging scenarios.

contributions: Operationalization of the DC/IC/UC feature taxonomy as the certification subspace for LLM-based IDS.
Demonstration that noise-augmented fine-tuning is essential for noise stability and meaningful certified accuracy in LLM-IDS.
Development of Traffic-Aware Randomized Smoothing (TA-RS) that injects noise only into attacker-controllable features during training and certification.
Empirical validation of TA-RS achieving up to 100% certified accuracy with large certified radii on multiple benchmark datasets.
limitations: TA-RS requires dataset-specific noise-augmented fine-tuning; pretrained LLM knowledge does not transfer without traffic-aware tuning.
The method fails on challenging datasets like RT-IoT2022 under default fine-tuning and needs increased noise augmentation to recover.
Certification sample counts are limited (N=200) due to LLM inference cost, resulting in conservative confidence bounds.
The approach assumes accurate identification of attacker-controllable features, which may be dataset-dependent and require domain expertise.
open_questions: How to improve noise stability of LLM-based IDS models to reduce reliance on heavy noise augmentation?
Can TA-RS be extended to certify robustness under more complex or adaptive attacker models beyond DC subspace perturbations?
What are the trade-offs between certification tightness and computational cost for large-scale LLM-IDS?
How to generalize the DC/IC/UC taxonomy and certification framework to other network security tasks or heterogeneous traffic representations?

papers.title: DataShield: Uncovering Risky Fine-Tuning Data Across LLMs Through Consensus Subspace Alignment
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) on domain-specific datasets has become a standard paradigm for adapting LLMs to specialized applications. However, recent work has shown that even fine-tuning on benign task-specific data can substantially weaken the safety capabilities of LLMs. While existing efforts have made progress in identifying data responsible for safety degradation, they usually rely on a single mean vector computed over a specific model with its tokenizer to represent the safety direction, which limits both the effectiveness and transferability of their risk assessment measures. To address these limitations, we propose DataShield, a data assessment framework that identifies risky fine-tuning samples and response segments through consensus subspace alignment over joint safety-critical semantic spaces derived from multiple safety-aligned LLMs. Within these spaces, DataShield extracts consensus safe and unsafe subspaces using semantic spectral decomposition over safe and unsafe data representations. The risk of a data sample or segment is then estimated by measuring its relative alignment with the unsafe and safe subspaces, enabling both sample-level filtering and fine-grained segment-level masking. Compared with state-of-the-art filtering and masking baselines, DataShield reduces ASR by 14.6\% with sample filtering and 32.3\% with segment masking, while preserving downstream utility and avoiding target-model-specific risk computation.

summary.takeaway: DataShield improves LLM fine-tuning safety by identifying risky data samples and segments through consensus subspace alignment across multiple safety-aligned models, outperforming prior methods in reducing attack success rates while preserving utility.
summary.problem: Fine-tuning LLMs on domain-specific data can degrade their safety capabilities, and existing data filtering methods lack transferability and granularity due to reliance on single-model mean vectors and tokenizer-dependent token-level risk estimation.
summary.method: DataShield constructs consensus safe and unsafe subspaces via semantic spectral decomposition over safety-critical representations from multiple LLMs, estimating risk by measuring alignment with these subspaces to enable sample-level filtering and segment-level masking.
summary.evidence: Experiments show DataShield reduces attack success rate (ASR) by 14.6% with sample filtering and 32.3% with segment masking compared to state-of-the-art baselines, while maintaining downstream task utility and avoiding target-model-specific risk computations.
summary.limitations: The paper does not provide explicit limitations or failure cases of DataShield, nor detailed analysis on computational overhead or performance on diverse downstream tasks beyond safety metrics.
summary.why_for_you: DataShield offers a transferable, model-agnostic approach to mitigate safety degradation during LLM fine-tuning, addressing key challenges in trustworthy LLM deployment by enabling reusable risk assessment across architectures and tokenizers.

signals.text: DataShield leverages semantic spectral decomposition to extract consensus safe and unsafe subspaces from multiple safety-aligned LLMs, capturing diverse safety-related directions beyond single mean vector representations.

The framework applies two intervention modes: DataShield-Sp for sample-level filtering by removing the top-risk samples, and DataShield-Sm for segment-level masking by masking high-risk response segments identified via tokenizer-independent segmentation.

Compared to state-of-the-art baselines, DataShield achieves a 14.6% reduction in attack success rate with sample filtering and a 32.3% reduction with segment masking, demonstrating improved safety preservation without sacrificing downstream utility.

deep_dive.overview: DataShield addresses the challenge of safety degradation in fine-tuned LLMs by proposing a data-centric risk assessment framework that overcomes limitations of prior methods relying on single-model, mean-vector-based risk estimates and tokenizer-dependent token-level masking. It constructs joint safety-critical semantic spaces by aggregating representations from multiple safety-aligned LLMs with diverse architectures. Through semantic spectral decomposition, DataShield extracts consensus safe and unsafe subspaces that capture richer safety semantics. Risk scores for fine-tuning samples and response segments are computed by measuring their alignment with these subspaces, enabling both sample-level filtering and fine-grained segment-level masking. This approach is model-agnostic and reusable across different target models and tokenizers. Empirical results demonstrate that DataShield significantly reduces harmful behavior compliance rates compared to existing filtering and masking baselines, while preserving downstream task performance. This establishes DataShield as an effective and transferable solution for mitigating safety risks in LLM fine-tuning.

methodology.title: Construction of Consensus Safe and Unsafe Subspaces
methodology.detail: DataShield uses multiple safety-aligned LLMs as source models to extract safety-critical hidden states from selected layers identified via an over-refusal probing dataset. Semantic spectral decomposition is applied to safe and unsafe data representations to derive consensus safe and unsafe subspaces capturing diverse safety-related directions.

methodology.title: Sample-Level Filtering (DataShield-Sp)
methodology.detail: For each fine-tuning sample, DataShield computes a risk score by averaging alignment gaps between the sample's representation and the consensus safe and unsafe subspaces across all source models. The top fraction ρ of samples with highest risk scores are removed from the fine-tuning dataset.

methodology.title: Segment-Level Masking (DataShield-Sm)
methodology.detail: Responses are split into tokenizer-independent raw-text segments using NLP tools. Each segment's risk is computed from autoregressive risk increments based on alignment with consensus subspaces. The top fraction ρ of high-risk segments are masked during fine-tuning to mitigate safety degradation.

methodology.title: Reusable Risk Estimation Across Models
methodology.detail: Risk measurement relies solely on fixed source models and their consensus subspaces, enabling the filtered or masked datasets to be reused for fine-tuning different target LLMs without recomputing risk, thus improving transferability and reducing computational cost.

mechanism.title: Consensus Subspace Alignment via Semantic Spectral Decomposition
mechanism.detail: DataShield aligns safety-critical semantic spaces from multiple LLMs by decomposing representations of safe and unsafe data into orthogonal subspaces. This spectral decomposition captures multiple safety-related directions rather than a single mean vector, enabling more robust and transferable risk estimation.

experiments.title: Evaluation of Sample Filtering and Segment Masking
experiments.detail: Experiments conducted on multiple LLM architectures demonstrate that DataShield-Sp reduces attack success rate by 14.6% and DataShield-Sm by 32.3% compared to state-of-the-art baselines, while preserving downstream task utility measured on domain-specific datasets.

experiments.title: Ablation on Tokenizer-Independent Segmentation
experiments.detail: DataShield uses NLP tools such as Jieba, NLTK, and spaCy to split responses into raw-text segments independent of model tokenizers, addressing tokenization mismatch issues and improving the transferability of segment-level masking across different LLMs.

findings.title: Improved Safety Preservation
findings.detail: DataShield significantly lowers harmful behavior compliance rates in fine-tuned LLMs, achieving a 14.6% ASR reduction with sample filtering and 32.3% with segment masking compared to prior methods relying on single-model risk estimates.

findings.title: Transferability Across Models and Tokenizers
findings.detail: By constructing consensus subspaces from multiple source models and using tokenizer-independent segmentation, DataShield's risk assessments and interventions generalize well across different target LLM architectures and tokenizers.

findings.title: Preservation of Downstream Utility
findings.detail: Despite aggressive filtering and masking of risky data, DataShield maintains the utility of fine-tuned models on downstream tasks, avoiding the trade-off between safety and performance observed in some prior approaches.

contributions: Proposed a novel consensus subspace alignment framework for safety risk estimation in fine-tuning data using multiple safety-aligned LLMs.
Developed semantic spectral decomposition to extract consensus safe and unsafe subspaces capturing diverse safety semantics.
Introduced sample-level filtering and tokenizer-independent segment-level masking interventions to mitigate safety degradation.
Demonstrated significant improvements in reducing harmful behavior compliance rates while preserving downstream utility.
Provided a reusable, model-agnostic risk assessment method that avoids target-model-specific computations.
limitations: No explicit discussion of computational overhead or scalability of DataShield's spectral decomposition and multi-model alignment.
Lack of detailed analysis on performance across a wide range of downstream tasks beyond safety metrics.
No reported failure cases or limitations in handling certain types of risky data or model architectures.
Unclear how DataShield performs under adversarially crafted fine-tuning data or evolving safety definitions.
open_questions: How does DataShield scale with increasing numbers and diversity of source models for consensus subspace construction?
Can the framework be extended to dynamically update consensus subspaces during continual fine-tuning or model updates?
What are the trade-offs between segment-level masking granularity and downstream task performance in different application domains?
How robust is DataShield against adversarial attempts to evade detection by manipulating fine-tuning data semantics?

papers.title: Beyond Score Prediction: LLM-Based Essay Scoring and Feedback Generation via Reinforcement Learning with Rubric Rewards
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been widely applied to automated essay scoring (AES) and automated feedback generation (AFG). However, existing studies rely primarily on prompt engineering or supervised fine-tuning, while systematic research on reinforcement learning (RL) post-training and automated evaluation of feedback quality remains limited. We propose RLAES, a unified LLM framework that jointly optimizes essay scoring and feedback generation through RL. To make feedback quality measurable, interpretable, and usable for training, we introduce Rubric-based Feedback Evaluation (RFE), an essay-grounded feedback evaluation framework comprising 166 fine-grained binary rubric items and an LLM-as-judge. Building on RFE, we propose Adaptive Gated Feedback Optimization (AGFO), which activates rubric-based feedback rewards on demand during RL, reducing evaluation overhead while improving feedback quality. We also propose Adjacent Contrastive Reasoning (ACR) to improve ordinal score calibration by explicitly contrasting adjacent score levels. Experimental results show that the RFE framework captures essay-feedback consistency, exhibits strong pairwise discriminative power, and closely aligns with expert preferences. On the ASAP benchmark, RLAES-AGFO achieves the best scoring performance among LLM-based methods (QWK = 0.803), while maintaining feedback quality comparable to GPT-5.5 and avoiding the feedback degradation observed under score-only RL. Code and datasets are publicly available at https://github.com/hellomuyi/RLAES.

summary.takeaway: RLAES, a unified LLM framework using reinforcement learning with rubric-based rewards, jointly optimizes essay scoring and feedback generation, achieving state-of-the-art scoring and high-quality feedback.
summary.problem: Existing AES and AFG methods rely mainly on prompt engineering or supervised fine-tuning, lacking systematic RL post-training and automated, scalable feedback quality evaluation.
summary.method: RLAES integrates Rubric-based Feedback Evaluation (RFE) with 166 binary rubric items and an LLM-as-judge, Adaptive Gated Feedback Optimization (AGFO) to reduce evaluation overhead, and Adjacent Contrastive Reasoning (ACR) for score calibration, optimized via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO).
summary.evidence: On the ASAP benchmark, RLAES-AGFO achieves the best LLM-based scoring performance (QWK=0.803) and feedback quality comparable to GPT-5.5, while avoiding feedback degradation seen in score-only RL.
summary.limitations: Feedback evaluation is computationally expensive, requiring gating mechanisms; evaluation was conducted on a single fold due to budget constraints, limiting generalizability.
summary.why_for_you: This work advances trustworthy LLM applications in education by providing a scalable, interpretable RL framework that jointly improves scoring accuracy and feedback quality with automated rubric-based evaluation.

signals.text: RFE framework uses 166 fine-grained binary rubric items evaluated by an LLM-as-judge to measure feedback quality, enabling interpretable and structured reward signals for RL.

AGFO adaptively gates the activation of feedback rewards during RL training, invoking the expensive LLM-as-judge only every n steps and only when feedback quality is below a threshold, reducing overhead by 83%.
Score-only RL training degrades feedback quality significantly (RFE score drops from 0.6978 to 0.5608), whereas joint optimization with AGFO maintains high feedback quality comparable to GPT-5.5.

deep_dive.overview: The paper addresses the challenge of jointly optimizing automated essay scoring (AES) and automated feedback generation (AFG) using large language models (LLMs). Prior work focused on prompt engineering or supervised fine-tuning, lacking systematic reinforcement learning (RL) approaches and scalable feedback evaluation. The authors propose RLAES, which integrates a novel Rubric-based Feedback Evaluation (RFE) framework comprising 166 binary rubric items assessed by an LLM-as-judge, enabling interpretable and measurable feedback quality. To mitigate the computational cost of frequent feedback evaluation, Adaptive Gated Feedback Optimization (AGFO) selectively activates feedback rewards during RL training based on a threshold, reducing overhead by 83%. Additionally, Adjacent Contrastive Reasoning (ACR) improves ordinal score calibration by contrasting adjacent score levels. Experiments on the ASAP dataset demonstrate that RLAES-AGFO achieves superior scoring performance (QWK=0.803) among LLM-based methods and maintains feedback quality comparable to GPT-5.5, avoiding the feedback degradation observed in score-only RL. This unified RL framework advances trustworthy AES and AFG by providing scalable, interpretable, and jointly optimized scoring and feedback generation.

methodology.title: Rubric-Based Feedback Evaluation (RFE)
methodology.detail: RFE decomposes feedback quality into 166 fine-grained binary rubric items, each evaluated independently by an LLM-as-judge, producing a structured reward signal for RL. This framework enables interpretable, essay-grounded feedback evaluation that aligns with expert preferences.

methodology.title: Adaptive Gated Feedback Optimization (AGFO)
methodology.detail: AGFO uses Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to jointly optimize scoring and feedback rewards. It adaptively gates feedback reward activation every n steps, invoking the LLM-as-judge only if the feedback reward falls below a threshold τ, reducing computational cost while maintaining feedback quality.

methodology.title: Adjacent Contrastive Reasoning (ACR)
methodology.detail: ACR improves ordinal score calibration by explicitly contrasting model outputs at adjacent score levels, enhancing the model's ability to discriminate fine-grained score differences and improving scoring accuracy.

methodology.title: Reinforcement Learning Setup
methodology.detail: The model is trained with GRPO using a combined reward of score accuracy and feedback quality. The score reward is scaled by a factor α and normalized by the score range. Feedback rewards are computed via RFE. Training uses LoRA for parameter-efficient fine-tuning on Qwen3.5-9B with a batch size of 8, learning rate 2e-5, and cosine scheduler.

mechanism.title: Rubric Reward Computation
mechanism.detail: The rubric reward r(x, ŷ) is computed as a weighted average of binary rubric item indicators cj(x, ŷ), where each cj is assigned by an LLM-as-judge independently. This decomposes complex feedback quality into assessable components, enabling structured RL rewards.

mechanism.title: Adaptive Gating Mechanism
mechanism.detail: Every n training steps, the feedback reward is computed; if it is below threshold τ, the gate remains open to optimize feedback; otherwise, feedback reward is skipped to save computation. This balances training efficiency and feedback quality.

experiments.title: Dataset and Evaluation
experiments.detail: Experiments use the ASAP dataset with 12,978 essays across 8 prompts, employing five-fold cross-validation with joint prompt training. Scoring is evaluated by quadratic weighted kappa (QWK), and feedback quality by RFE scores using GPT-5.5 as the LLM judge.

experiments.title: Baselines
experiments.detail: Baselines include LLM prompt engineering methods (GPT-3.5, GPT-4 with rubric and few-shot prompting, Llama-3-8B-Instruct) and post-training methods. The base model for RLAES is Qwen3.5-9B fine-tuned with LoRA.

experiments.title: Training Setup
experiments.detail: RLAES is trained for 25 epochs with GRPO, batch size 8, learning rate 2e-5, and temperature 0.9 for rollout sampling. Feedback reward weight λf=1, score scaling α=0.1, gating period n=30, and threshold τ=0.8.

findings.title: Superior Scoring Performance
findings.detail: RLAES-AGFO achieves a QWK of 0.803 on ASAP, outperforming all LLM-based baselines including GPT-4 variants and prompt engineering methods.

findings.title: Maintained Feedback Quality
findings.detail: RLAES-AGFO attains an average RFE feedback score of 0.8399, comparable to GPT-5.5's 0.8334, while score-only RL degrades feedback quality significantly to 0.5608.

findings.title: Efficiency Gains
findings.detail: AGFO reduces the computational cost of feedback evaluation by approximately 83% compared to full feedback optimization, enabling practical RL training with rubric rewards.

findings.title: Joint Optimization Benefits
findings.detail: Joint optimization of scoring and feedback rewards via AGFO improves both scoring accuracy and feedback quality without trade-offs, unlike score-only RL.

contributions: Proposed RLAES, a unified RL framework jointly optimizing AES and AFG with rubric-based rewards.
Developed Rubric-based Feedback Evaluation (RFE) with 166 binary rubric items and LLM-as-judge for interpretable feedback quality measurement.
Introduced Adaptive Gated Feedback Optimization (AGFO) to reduce feedback evaluation overhead during RL training.
Designed Adjacent Contrastive Reasoning (ACR) to improve ordinal score calibration.
Demonstrated state-of-the-art scoring and high-quality feedback generation on the ASAP benchmark.
limitations: Feedback evaluation using LLM-as-judge is computationally expensive, necessitating gating mechanisms.
Feedback evaluation was conducted on a single fold due to budget constraints, limiting robustness assessment.
The approach depends on the quality and coverage of the predefined rubric items, which may not capture all feedback nuances.
No explicit mechanism or theoretical analysis is provided for the interaction between scoring and feedback rewards.
open_questions: How well does RLAES generalize to other essay datasets or languages beyond ASAP?
Can the rubric-based evaluation framework be extended or adapted to other open-ended NLP tasks?
What are the effects of different rubric item designs or weighting schemes on feedback quality and scoring accuracy?
How can human-in-the-loop feedback be integrated to further improve rubric reward reliability and reduce bias?

papers.title: On-Policy Delta Distillation
papers.abstract: On-policy distillation is an alternative post-training method in reinforcement learning that alleviates the constraints imposed by reward models by providing token-level supervision from a teacher model. Although on-policy distillation has been studied and applied across various settings, its fundamental design remains underexplored. In this paper, we introduce a new distillation reward, termed the delta signal, instead of directly imitating the teacher's output distribution. The delta signal is defined as the difference between the teacher model and its base model prior to instruction tuning for reasoning capability. It therefore captures the changes induced by reasoning tuning and provides a more direct signal for transferring reasoning capabilities. Using extensive empirical evidence, we show that the delta signal substantially improves on-policy distillation and refer to the new distillation method as On-Policy Delta Distillation (OPD$^2$). Experiments across mathematics, science, and code-reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that OPD$^2$ consistently outperforms conventional on-policy distillation, enabling reasoning LLMs to achieve strong performance with only a short post-training period. Code will be available at https://github.com/naver-ai/opd2

summary.takeaway: On-Policy Delta Distillation (OPD2), which uses the delta signal between a teacher and its base model, significantly improves reasoning capability transfer in on-policy distillation.
summary.problem: Conventional on-policy distillation uses the teacher's output distribution directly, which may not effectively capture the reasoning knowledge gained during instruction tuning.
summary.method: OPD2 defines a new distillation reward as the difference (delta signal) between the teacher model and its base model prior to reasoning tuning, focusing on the learning trajectory for reasoning capability.
summary.evidence: Extensive experiments on multiple benchmarks across Math, Science, and Code domains show OPD2 consistently outperforms both conventional OPD and advanced ExOPD methods across various model sizes.
summary.limitations: The paper does not address extensions of OPD signals beyond sampled tokens and does not provide detailed mechanism equations for the delta signal.
summary.why_for_you: OPD2 offers a novel, empirically validated approach to enhance on-policy distillation for reasoning LLMs, relevant for improving post-training methods in reinforcement learning.

signals.text: The delta signal, defined as the difference between the reasoning-tuned teacher and its base model, captures the knowledge gained during instruction tuning, providing a more direct supervision signal for reasoning capability transfer.

OPD2 applies on-policy distillation by scoring student-generated tokens using the delta signal rather than the teacher's raw output probabilities, preserving the student's original knowledge while enhancing reasoning skills.

Empirical results on Qwen3 and Gemma4 models across 14 benchmarks show OPD2 achieves substantial improvements over OPD and ExOPD, with gains in pass@1 metrics in Math, Science, and Code tasks, demonstrating the effectiveness of the delta signal.

deep_dive.overview: This paper addresses the fundamental design of on-policy distillation (OPD) in reinforcement learning for large language models, focusing on improving the transfer of reasoning capabilities. Traditional OPD uses the teacher's output distribution as a reward signal, which may not isolate the reasoning knowledge acquired during instruction tuning. The authors propose On-Policy Delta Distillation (OPD2), which leverages the delta signal—the difference between the teacher model and its base model before reasoning tuning—as a more direct and informative reward. This approach captures the learning trajectory of reasoning tuning, enabling more effective knowledge transfer. Extensive experiments on multiple reasoning domains (Math, Science, Code) and benchmarks demonstrate that OPD2 consistently outperforms conventional OPD and the advanced ExOPD method across various model sizes and architectures. The results validate that the delta signal provides a richer supervision signal, leading to improved reasoning performance with a short post-training period. The paper contributes a novel distillation reward design and comprehensive empirical validation, positioning OPD2 as a significant advancement in on-policy distillation for reasoning LLMs.

methodology.title: Delta Signal Computation
methodology.detail: Compute the delta signal as the difference between the teacher model's output distribution after reasoning tuning and its base model's output distribution prior to tuning. This delta captures the reasoning knowledge gained during instruction tuning.

methodology.title: On-Policy Distillation Training
methodology.detail: Generate sequences using the student model and apply the delta signal as a reward to sampled tokens. Tokens aligned with positive delta values are reinforced, while those with negative values are suppressed, preserving the student's original knowledge.

methodology.title: Multi-Domain Dataset Construction
methodology.detail: Construct a mixed training dataset by sampling questions from Math, Science, and Code reasoning domains to ensure broad applicability and robustness of the distillation method.

methodology.title: Evaluation Protocol
methodology.detail: Evaluate models on 14 benchmarks spanning three domains using pass@1 metrics, comparing OPD2 against baseline OPD, ExOPD, and original models in both non-thinking and thinking generation modes.

methodology.title: Training Configuration
methodology.detail: Train models for 100 optimization steps with AdamW optimizer, learning rate 5e-6, cosine decay, batch sizes 256-288, gradient clipping, and scaled rewards to stabilize training without KL regularization.

mechanism.title: Delta Signal as Learning Trajectory
mechanism.detail: The delta signal represents the difference in output probabilities between the teacher model after reasoning tuning and its base model before tuning, effectively encoding the knowledge changes induced by instruction tuning. No explicit equations are provided, but the delta acts as a refined reward signal focusing on reasoning capability.

experiments.title: Model and Dataset Setup
experiments.detail: Use Qwen3 (1.7B, 4B, 8B) and Gemma4-E4B as student models with corresponding larger teacher models from the same family. Train on a mixed dataset of Math, Science, and Code questions, evaluating on 14 benchmarks with pass@1 metric.

experiments.title: Baseline Comparisons
experiments.detail: Compare OPD2 against conventional OPD and ExOPD, an advanced on-policy distillation method that amplifies extrapolation signals using teacher-base models, to assess relative performance improvements.

experiments.title: Generation Modes
experiments.detail: Evaluate both non-thinking mode (no explicit reasoning traces) and thinking mode (with reasoning traces) for Qwen3 models, while Gemma4 is evaluated only in thinking mode to assess OPD2's effectiveness across generation styles.

experiments.title: Training and Hardware
experiments.detail: Train models on NVIDIA H100 GPUs with multi-node setups for larger models, using 100 optimization steps and effective batch sizes of 256-288, ensuring reproducibility and scalability of OPD2 training.

findings.title: Performance Gains Across Domains
findings.detail: OPD2 consistently outperforms OPD and ExOPD on Math, Science, and Code benchmarks, with improvements in pass@1 scores across all tested model sizes, demonstrating the delta signal's effectiveness in transferring reasoning knowledge.

findings.title: Effectiveness in Non-Thinking Mode
findings.detail: In non-thinking mode, where reasoning is less explicit, OPD2 achieves substantial improvements over baselines, indicating its ability to enhance reasoning capabilities even without explicit reasoning traces.

findings.title: Robustness Across Model Sizes
findings.detail: OPD2 shows consistent performance gains from smaller (1.7B) to larger (8B) Qwen3 models, suggesting scalability and general applicability of the delta signal approach.

findings.title: Short Post-Training Period
findings.detail: OPD2 enables strong reasoning performance improvements with only 100 optimization steps, highlighting its efficiency as a post-training method.

contributions: Introduction of the delta signal as a novel distillation reward capturing reasoning tuning knowledge.
Development of On-Policy Delta Distillation (OPD2) method leveraging the delta signal for improved reasoning capability transfer.
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple reasoning domains, benchmarks, and model sizes demonstrating OPD2's superiority over OPD and ExOPD.
Demonstration that OPD2 achieves strong reasoning performance with a short post-training period, enhancing efficiency.
Provision of an open-source codebase for reproducibility and further research.
limitations: The paper does not explore extending the delta signal beyond sampled tokens or alternative reward designs.
No explicit mathematical formulation or theoretical analysis of the delta signal mechanism is provided.
Evaluation is limited to specific model families (Qwen3 and Gemma4) and may not generalize to all LLM architectures.
The impact of OPD2 on generation diversity or other qualitative aspects beyond pass@1 metrics is not discussed.
open_questions: How can the delta signal be extended or combined with other reward signals beyond sampled tokens for further performance gains?
What theoretical guarantees or formal analyses can be developed to explain why the delta signal effectively transfers reasoning knowledge?
Can OPD2 be generalized to other LLM architectures or domains beyond Math, Science, and Code reasoning?
How does OPD2 affect other aspects of model behavior such as generation diversity, robustness, or alignment with human preferences?

papers.title: Inference-Time Steering for Cross-Lingual Factual Consistency in LLMs
papers.abstract: Although Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate remarkable multilingual fluency, their internal knowledge representations remain disproportionately biased toward high-resource languages. This leads to cross-lingual factual inconsistency, where they shift their empirical answer distributions based solely on the prompt language. We investigate whether these biases can be mitigated at inference time, forcing an English-prompted model to answer as if it were queried in target languages (German, Spanish, Bulgarian), and evaluate four intervention strategies: zero-shot contextual steering (persona prompting), internal representation manipulation via Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA), and lightweight weight modification via Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) trained on benchmark-derived factual data as well as conceptual generalization data. To assess alignment, we curate a multilingual factual dataset alongside a novel generalization benchmark comprising culturally rooted queries to determine whether factual interventions transfer to broader target-centric preferences. Experiments on Gemma 3 12B Instruct reveal persona prompting to be the strongest overall intervention, balancing efficacy, safety, and out-of-domain generalization. While CAA yields sharp inconsistency benchmark shifts, it is configuration-sensitive and risks knowledge degradation. DPO-based adapters offer permanent, yet narrower and less transferable gains. These findings suggest that cross-lingual inconsistency is at least partly a selection problem, and that simple contextual interventions may outperform more invasive methods for robust, transferable alignment.
papers.comment: 8 pages (21 in total), 2 figures, 4 tables. Original manuscript for a Guided Research project conducted at the Technical University of Munich, detailing the complete methodology, full data pipeline, and comprehensive experimental results. A related, condensed subset of this work was subsequently adapted and published at the StereACuLT 2026 workshop

summary.takeaway: Zero-shot persona prompting effectively mitigates cross-lingual factual inconsistency in LLMs at inference time, outperforming deeper mechanistic and parameter-based interventions in robustness and transferability.
summary.problem: Large Language Models exhibit cross-lingual factual inconsistency due to biased internal knowledge representations favoring high-resource languages, leading to unreliable multilingual factual recall.
summary.method: The paper evaluates four inference-time interventions—persona prompting, Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA), and Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) adapters trained on benchmark and generalization data—to steer English-prompted LLMs toward target language factual preferences.
summary.evidence: Experiments on Gemma 3 12B Instruct show persona prompting consistently improves Jensen–Shannon distance and target preference metrics across German, Spanish, and Bulgarian, with statistically significant gains and superior safety and generalization compared to CAA and DPO.
summary.limitations: CAA steering is highly sensitive to hyperparameter tuning and risks knowledge degradation, while DPO adapters yield narrower, less transferable improvements; the study is limited to Gemma 3 12B and three target languages.
summary.why_for_you: This work provides a rigorous comparative analysis of inference-time steering methods for cross-lingual factual alignment, offering practical, lightweight interventions relevant for trustworthy and efficient multilingual LLM deployment.

signals.text: Persona prompting significantly reduces cross-lingual Jensen–Shannon distance (JSD) in German and Bulgarian, achieving p < 0.05 and p < 0.01 respectively, indicating effective alignment of English-prompted model outputs with target language factual distributions.

Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) manipulates the model’s residual stream by adding a steering vector derived from contrast pairs of English-preferred and target-preferred completions, enabling mechanistic preference realignment during inference.

CAA’s effectiveness depends on precise layer selection and multiplier scaling, with optimal configurations varying by language; misconfiguration can degrade performance, as seen with Spanish under broad contrast pair settings where JSD worsened.

deep_dive.overview: The paper addresses the problem of cross-lingual factual inconsistency in LLMs, where models biased toward English produce divergent factual answers when prompted in different languages. It hypothesizes that such biases can be mitigated at inference time by steering the model’s output distribution to reflect target language preferences without costly retraining. To test this, the authors curate a multilingual factual dataset and a novel cultural generalization benchmark, then evaluate four intervention strategies on Gemma 3 12B Instruct: zero-shot persona prompting, Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA), and Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) adapters trained on benchmark and generalization data. Persona prompting, a shallow contextual intervention, consistently improves alignment metrics and generalizes well, suggesting the model already encodes target knowledge but defaults to English-centric answers. CAA, a mechanistic activation manipulation, achieves strong but fragile improvements sensitive to hyperparameters. DPO adapters provide permanent but narrower gains. These results support the view that cross-lingual inconsistency is partly a selection problem and that simple contextual cues can outperform more invasive methods for robust, transferable alignment.

methodology.title: Persona Prompting
methodology.detail: A zero-shot contextual steering method that augments English prompts with natural language instructions to adopt the perspective of a target language demographic, leveraging in-context learning to shift output distributions without modifying model parameters or activations.

methodology.title: Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA)
methodology.detail: An inference-time intervention that adds a directional steering vector to the model’s residual stream activations, computed from contrast pairs of English-preferred and target-preferred completions, to mechanistically realign the model’s internal representations toward target language preferences.

methodology.title: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) Adapters
methodology.detail: Lightweight parameter-efficient fine-tuning adapters trained on preference triples derived from benchmark or generalization datasets, optimizing the model to prefer target language completions over English-centric ones, enabling permanent but narrower alignment shifts.

methodology.title: Multilingual Factual Dataset and Generalization Benchmark
methodology.detail: A curated dataset of atomic factual triples across six languages designed for repeated-sampling evaluation of answer distributions, and a culturally rooted generalization benchmark with 50 second-person multiple-choice queries per target language to test transfer of interventions beyond benchmark facts.

mechanism.title: Cross-Lingual Factual Inconsistency as a Selection Problem
mechanism.detail: The paper posits that LLMs share a common semantic space for multilingual inputs but exhibit biased output distributions due to the final language transition step favoring English-centric knowledge; thus, inference-time interventions can steer output selection without altering underlying representations.

experiments.title: Baseline Cross-Lingual Inconsistency Measurement
experiments.detail: Evaluated four state-of-the-art LLMs (Gemma 3 12B, gpt-oss-20b, Qwen 3 30B-A3B, Llama 4 Maverick) on a multilingual factual benchmark using repeated open-ended sampling and Jensen–Shannon distance to quantify answer distribution shifts across English, German, Spanish, Bulgarian, Korean, and Swedish.

experiments.title: Intervention Evaluation on Gemma 3 12B Instruct
experiments.detail: Compared persona prompting, CAA steering, and DPO adapters trained on benchmark and generalization data across three contrast pair strategies (v0, v1, v2), measuring improvements in JSD and target preference metrics, statistical significance, and transfer to a novel cultural generalization benchmark.

findings.title: Effectiveness of Persona Prompting
findings.detail: Persona prompting improved cross-lingual alignment in 8 of 9 cases, with statistically significant JSD reductions for German (p < 0.05, CLES=0.705) and Bulgarian (p < 0.01, CLES=0.672–0.690), demonstrating that simple contextual cues can induce substantial preference shifts without parameter changes.

findings.title: CAA Steering Performance and Fragility
findings.detail: CAA improved JSD in 8 of 9 cases with large effect sizes for Bulgarian (p < 0.01, CLES=0.741) and German (p < 0.01, CLES=0.705), but required careful tuning of intervention layer and multiplier; broader contrast sets (v2) sometimes degraded performance, indicating sensitivity and risk of knowledge degradation.

findings.title: DPO Adapter Gains and Transfer
findings.detail: DPO adapters trained on benchmark-derived data provided permanent alignment improvements but with narrower scope and less transfer to out-of-benchmark cultural generalization compared to prompting, highlighting trade-offs between permanence and generality.

contributions: Curated a high-quality multilingual factual dataset spanning six languages for distributional evaluation of cross-lingual factual consistency.
Developed a novel culturally rooted generalization benchmark to test transfer of alignment interventions beyond benchmark-specific facts.
Conducted a rigorous comparative study of four inference-time steering methods—persona prompting, CAA, and two DPO adapter variants—on Gemma 3 12B Instruct.
Demonstrated that zero-shot persona prompting is the strongest overall intervention balancing efficacy, safety, and out-of-domain generalization.
Provided evidence that cross-lingual inconsistency is partly a selection problem addressable by simple contextual interventions rather than invasive parameter updates.
limitations: CAA steering is highly sensitive to hyperparameter choices and can degrade model knowledge if misconfigured.
DPO adapters yield narrower and less transferable gains compared to prompting, limiting their generalization to broader cultural contexts.
Experiments are limited to the Gemma 3 12B Instruct model and three target languages, restricting generalizability to other architectures or languages.
The study does not provide mechanistic explanations beyond the steering vector concept, leaving deeper causal understanding of cross-lingual bias unaddressed.
open_questions: Can inference-time steering methods be effectively generalized to larger or different LLM architectures beyond Gemma 3 12B?
How can the fragility and hyperparameter sensitivity of CAA be mitigated to ensure safe and robust mechanistic interventions?
What are the underlying representational mechanisms causing cross-lingual factual inconsistency beyond selection bias?
Can permanent parameter updates be designed to combine the transferability of prompting with the permanence of DPO adapters?

papers.title: A Geometric Perspective on Stabilizing Value Conflict Resolution
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often struggle to navigate value conflicts when trained with the compressed scalar rewards of Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF). To address this challenge, we investigate how chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning can help improve performance in this domain. Geometrically, we show that CoT correlates with further smoothing the model's loss landscape in its sharpest direction, helping resolve the optimization instability of traditional scalar rewards. We also demonstrate via relevant downstream benchmarks that value conflict-focused CoT may generalize to different kinds of moral reasoning, demonstrating that this CoT has the potential to be an effective mechanism for better moral reasoning. To capitalize on this potential, we create a new value conflict-focused CoT design that further smooths the sharpest direction of the loss landscape and increases moral reasoning performance. This finding shows that explicitly modifying and improving the design of reasoning dynamics offers a promising avenue for improving model performance on user requests with complex value conflicts, advancing pluralistic alignment in LLMs.
papers.comment: Accepted to ICML Workshop on High-Dimensional Learning Dynamics

summary.takeaway: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning smooths the sharpest direction of the LLM loss landscape, stabilizing value conflict resolution and improving moral reasoning performance.
summary.problem: LLMs trained with scalar rewards from RLHF struggle with unstable optimization and flawed moral reasoning when resolving conflicting human values.
summary.method: The authors design a value conflict-focused annealing-inspired CoT framework that mimics thermodynamic annealing phases to smooth the loss landscape and improve reasoning dynamics.
summary.evidence: Hessian top eigenvalue analysis shows annealing CoT achieves the lowest maximum curvature (λmax ≈ 1218), indicating the flattest minimum and best stability, with corresponding improved benchmark moral reasoning accuracy.
summary.limitations: Performance improvements from CoT are within the margin of error, and experiments focus on binary value conflicts without scaling to higher-dimensional pluralistic value spaces.
summary.why_for_you: This work provides a geometric and mechanistic understanding of how CoT reasoning dynamics can be explicitly designed to stabilize LLM training on value conflicts, advancing trustworthy pluralistic alignment.

signals.text: Annealing-inspired CoT reduces the top Hessian eigenvalue from 4083 (base RLHF) to 1218, indicating a much smoother loss landscape in the sharpest direction and more stable optimization.

The annealing CoT method structures reasoning into three cognitive phases—high-temperature exploration, cooling trade-off weighing, and low-temperature decisive action—mimicking thermodynamic annealing to resolve value conflicts.

Benchmark results on moral reasoning datasets show annealing CoT outperforms base RLHF, base SFT, and standard CoT models, achieving the highest accuracy by a larger margin, demonstrating improved moral reasoning capability.

deep_dive.overview: This paper addresses the instability and flawed moral reasoning in LLMs trained with scalar rewards from RLHF when resolving conflicting human values. The authors hypothesize that chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning can mitigate this by smoothing the loss landscape's sharpest direction, stabilizing optimization. They draw an analogy to geometric frustration in physics and thermodynamic annealing, designing an annealing-inspired CoT framework with three cognitive phases to guide the model from broad exploration to decisive trade-offs. Empirical Hessian analysis confirms that annealing CoT achieves the flattest minima, reducing the top eigenvalue significantly compared to base RLHF and standard CoT. Correspondingly, moral reasoning benchmarks show improved performance, although some gains are within error margins. The work highlights the importance of explicitly designing reasoning dynamics to improve pluralistic alignment and suggests that internal reasoning design complements external reward engineering. Limitations include focus on binary value conflicts and lack of scaling to more complex pluralistic environments.

methodology.title: Data Generation
methodology.detail: Prompts eliciting value conflicts were generated using the ConflictScope pipeline with Claude 3.5 Sonnet, covering diverse conflicting value pairs. An ensemble of LLMs (GPT 5 Nano, Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite, Claude 4.5 Haiku) generated two reasoning traces per prompt: a standard unstructured CoT and an annealing-inspired CoT with structured cognitive phases.

methodology.title: Annealing-inspired CoT Design
methodology.detail: The CoT reasoning is structured into three phases: (1) high-temperature broad exploration weighing values, (2) cooling phase weighing trade-offs, and (3) low-temperature decisive action making hierarchical trade-offs. This design mimics thermodynamic annealing to resolve geometric frustration in value conflicts.

methodology.title: Loss Landscape Analysis
methodology.detail: The authors analyze the Hessian top eigenvalue (λmax) of the loss landscape to quantify sharpness and stability. Lower λmax indicates a flatter, more stable minimum. They visualize 3D eigenplane loss landscapes by perturbing model weights along top eigenvectors to qualitatively assess optimization geometry.

methodology.title: Model Training and Evaluation
methodology.detail: Models trained include base RLHF, base supervised fine-tuning (SFT), standard CoT, and annealing CoT. Evaluation metrics include Hessian eigenvalues for stability and benchmark accuracy on moral reasoning datasets such as MMLU Moral Scenarios, DecodingTrust Machine Ethics, and SafetyBench.

mechanism.title: Geometric Frustration and Annealing Analogy
mechanism.detail: Value conflict resolution in LLMs is analogous to geometric frustration in condensed matter physics, where incompatible constraints create a rugged, spiky energy landscape. Annealing, a thermodynamic process of heating and gradual cooling, resolves frustration by guiding the system to a stable, low-energy configuration. The annealing-inspired CoT framework translates this principle into cognitive phases that smooth the loss landscape and stabilize optimization.

experiments.title: Loss Landscape Visualization and Hessian Analysis
experiments.detail: The authors visualize 3D loss landscapes along top Hessian eigenvectors for base RLHF, base SFT, standard CoT, and annealing CoT models. Quantitatively, the top eigenvalue λmax decreases from 4083.87 (base RLHF) to 1218.04 (annealing CoT), indicating progressive smoothing and stability.

experiments.title: Moral Reasoning Benchmark Evaluation
experiments.detail: Models are evaluated on multiple moral reasoning benchmarks including MMLU Moral Scenarios, DecodingTrust Machine Ethics, and SafetyBench. Annealing CoT achieves the highest accuracy (e.g., 41.67% on MMLU Moral Scenarios) outperforming base RLHF and standard CoT, demonstrating improved moral reasoning performance.

findings.title: Scalar Reward Optimization Instability
findings.detail: Direct scalar reward optimization via RLHF leads to a sharp, cliff-like loss landscape with a high top Hessian eigenvalue (~4083), indicating unstable value conflict resolution.

findings.title: Supervised Fine-Tuning Smoothing Effect
findings.detail: Supervised fine-tuning on responses reduces the top eigenvalue to ~1402, smoothing the loss landscape into a ravine-like shape and improving stability.

findings.title: CoT Further Smooths Loss Landscape
findings.detail: Standard CoT reduces the top eigenvalue further to ~1346, and annealing CoT achieves the lowest eigenvalue (~1218), indicating the flattest minima and most stable optimization.

findings.title: Performance Gains on Moral Reasoning
findings.detail: Annealing CoT outperforms other methods on moral reasoning benchmarks by a larger margin, e.g., 41.67% accuracy on MMLU Moral Scenarios compared to 24.67% for base RLHF, demonstrating improved moral reasoning capability.

contributions: Demonstration that value conflict-focused annealing CoT design flattens the sharpest direction of the loss landscape and improves moral reasoning performance.
Geometric analysis linking CoT reasoning dynamics to smoothing of the loss landscape beyond supervised fine-tuning effects.
Release of a new dataset and code for standard and annealing CoT reasoning traces on value conflict prompts.
Empirical evidence that scalar reward optimization is ill-equipped for stable value conflict resolution in LLMs.
Proposal of explicit reasoning dynamics design as a promising avenue for advancing pluralistic alignment.
limitations: Performance improvements from CoT are within the margin of error, limiting statistical significance.
Experiments focus on binary value conflicts without scaling to N-dimensional pluralistic value spaces.
No formal mapping of trade-offs between internal reasoning design and external reward engineering is provided.
Mechanistic explanations are analogical and lack formal mathematical modeling.
open_questions: How can CoT methods be scaled from binary to N-dimensional pluralistic value conflicts in LLMs?
What are the formal trade-offs between improving value conflict resolution via internal reasoning dynamics versus external RLHF reward design?
Can the annealing-inspired CoT framework be generalized to other forms of complex reasoning beyond moral value conflicts?
What are the precise mechanistic underpinnings linking loss landscape geometry changes to improved moral reasoning performance?

papers.title: Adopting Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards for Molecular Generation
papers.abstract: Leveraging large language models (LLMs) for molecular generation has shown remarkable potential in chemical and drug design. Current methods primarily rely on supervised training or fine-tuning with limited datasets, which are insufficient to capture complex molecular design objectives. While some approaches attempt to guide generation toward specific goals, they often lack direct optimization mechanisms, making it difficult to align generated molecules with desired properties. To tackle these challenges, we propose \textbf{LLMol}, a principled reinforcement learning framework that directly incorporates verifiable rewards for targeted molecule generation. The key insight is to formulate molecular design as a goal-conditioned sequence prediction task, where verifiable rewards serve as explicit supervision to drive generation toward desired objectives. LLMol follows a two-stage training paradigm combining supervised learning and reinforcement learning. In the first stage, large language models are supervised fine-tuned to capture chemical syntax and molecular distributions. In the second stage, we introduce Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR), which directly integrates property-based reward signals to guide molecular generation toward task-specific objectives. To address the high variance and instability common in discrete sequence optimization, we adopt Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), a stable on-policy algorithm that smooths reward signals and improves training robustness. This framework enables LLMol to effectively handle a range of molecular design tasks, including single-property targeting (e.g., penalized logP, QED) and structure-constrained optimization. Experimental results demonstrate that LLMol consistently outperforms existing methods, achieving higher success rates and improved efficiency across diverse molecular benchmarks.

summary.problem: Existing LLM-based molecular generation methods lack direct optimization mechanisms to align generated molecules with complex, multi-objective chemical design goals.
summary.method: LLMol formulates molecular design as a goal-conditioned sequence prediction task and applies Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to optimize property-based reward signals.

deep_dive.overview: LLMol addresses the challenge of aligning molecular generation with complex chemical objectives by framing molecular design as a goal-conditioned sequence prediction problem. It first fine-tunes a large language model (Qwen-3, 4B parameters) on molecular string data (simplified SELFIES) to learn chemical syntax and distributions. Subsequently, it applies Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) to directly optimize property-based reward functions, such as penalized logP and QED, using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to reduce variance and stabilize training. This two-stage approach enables precise control over molecular properties while preserving validity, novelty, and diversity. Experiments on the ZINC250K dataset demonstrate that LLMol significantly outperforms diverse baselines across multiple molecular generation tasks, achieving higher success rates and efficiency. The framework’s use of verifiable, deterministic rewards and stable policy optimization represents a principled advancement in LLM-driven molecular design.

methodology.title: Molecule Representation
methodology.detail: LLMol adopts a simplified SELFIES molecular string representation that removes square brackets and inserts spaces between semantic units, reducing token length and vocabulary complexity to improve LLM tokenization efficiency and modeling.
