methodology.detail: The base Qwen-3 4B parameter LLM is fine-tuned on over 200,000 molecules from ZINC250K using LoRA to reduce trainable parameters. The objective is to learn chemical syntax and molecular distributions, enabling valid and novel molecule generation.

methodology.title: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR)
methodology.detail: RLVR integrates explicit property-based reward functions computed via RDKit to guide molecular generation toward task-specific objectives. The policy is optimized using GRPO, an on-policy algorithm that uses group-based Monte Carlo rollouts and reward whitening to stabilize training.

methodology.title: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO)
methodology.detail: GRPO estimates relative advantages by comparing grouped rollout returns, avoiding the need for a critic model. It standardizes rewards through whitening and supports deterministic verifiable rewards, improving stability and exploration in discrete sequence optimization.

mechanism.title: Reward-Driven Goal-Conditioned Sequence Prediction
mechanism.detail: Molecular generation is formulated as a goal-conditioned sequence prediction task where the LLM generates molecular strings conditioned on desired property values. Verifiable reward functions provide explicit supervision signals to guide the policy toward molecules satisfying these properties.

experiments.title: Supervised Fine-Tuning Evaluation on ZINC250K

experiments.title: LogP Targeting Task
experiments.detail: LLMol is evaluated on generating molecules within a narrow logP range, achieving a 46.91% success rate compared to 0.46% for SFT-only and outperforming prior methods, while maintaining high diversity (0.893).

experiments.title: QED and Penalized logP Maximization
experiments.detail: LLMol optimizes drug-likeness metrics (QED and penalized logP) using RLVR, outperforming baselines in maximum scores and efficiency, with training times significantly reduced (2 hours for LLMol vs. up to 30 hours for others).

experiments.title: Similarity-Constrained Optimization
experiments.detail: LLMol demonstrates the ability to improve molecular properties while preserving structural similarity to known compounds, validating its applicability to constrained molecular design tasks.

findings.title: RLVR Significantly Improves Property Targeting
findings.detail: In logP targeting, RL-augmented LLMol achieves a 46.91% success rate, a 100x improvement over supervised fine-tuning alone (0.46%), demonstrating the effectiveness of verifiable reward integration.

findings.title: High Validity and Novelty Maintained
findings.detail: LLMol achieves 100% validity and novelty on ZINC250K, indicating that reinforcement learning does not degrade chemical correctness or exploration of novel molecules.

findings.title: Training Efficiency Gains
findings.detail: LLMol completes reinforcement learning training in approximately 2 hours, substantially faster than several baselines requiring up to 30 hours, highlighting the efficiency of GRPO and LoRA parameter reduction.

findings.title: Diversity Preservation
findings.detail: Despite optimization for specific properties, LLMol maintains a high diversity score (0.893), close to the LIMO baseline (0.914), ensuring broad chemical space exploration.

Introduced Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) to directly optimize property-based reward functions in molecular generation.
Developed Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), a stable on-policy RL algorithm that smooths reward signals and avoids critic models.
Demonstrated state-of-the-art performance on multiple molecular design tasks including logP targeting, QED maximization, and similarity-constrained optimization.
Adopted a simplified SELFIES representation to improve tokenization efficiency for LLM-based molecular modeling.

Limited evaluation on multi-property or multi-objective optimization beyond single-property and similarity constraints.
No detailed analysis of failure modes or robustness to noisy or conflicting reward signals.
Absence of mechanistic or theoretical analysis explaining why GRPO outperforms other RL algorithms in this context.

Can the GRPO algorithm be generalized or adapted to other discrete sequence generation domains beyond molecular design?
What are the effects of different verifiable reward function designs on the stability and convergence of RLVR?
How robust is LLMol to noisy or approximate reward signals derived from imperfect property predictors?

papers.title: PPL-Factory: Task-Aware and Budget-Aware Data Selection from Language Modeling to Reasoning
papers.abstract: Not all training samples contribute equally to large language model fine-tuning. Selecting informative training samples can reduce the computational cost while preserving downstream performance. Many existing data selection methods rely on indirect heuristics, such as data quality, diversity or reasoning trace length. However, the effectiveness of these fixed criteria is task-dependent and difficult to generalize across diverse downstream tasks. Perplexity-based data selection provides a simple and model-aware solution to estimate the sample difficulty, but existing approaches typically score the entire training sequence and ignore the difference in learning objectives of language modeling and reasoning tasks. In this paper, we propose PPL-Factory, a simple and interpretable data selection framework that combines task-aware perplexity-based scores and data budget-aware selection criteria. Experiments on GSM8K demonstrate that PPL-Factory outperforms other state-of-the-art data selection methods using only $1\%$ of the training set. With $10\%$ of the data, PPL-Factory exceeds full-data fine-tuning accuracy by 0.9 on GSM8K and 4.8 on MATH. Overall, our results demonstrate that task-aware and budget-aware perplexity-based selection provides an effective and applicable approach for efficient fine-tuning.

summary.takeaway: PPL-Factory effectively selects informative training samples for LLM fine-tuning, enhancing performance while reducing computational costs.
summary.problem: Existing data selection methods struggle with task dependency and computational efficiency in LLM fine-tuning.
summary.method: PPL-Factory combines task-aware perplexity-based scoring with budget-aware selection criteria for improved data selection.
summary.evidence: Experiments show PPL-Factory outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving 0.9 and 4.8 accuracy improvements on GSM8K and MATH with only 10% of the data.
summary.limitations: The paper does not address the performance of PPL-Factory under extremely low data budgets beyond the tested scenarios.
summary.why_for_you: This framework is crucial for optimizing data selection in LLMs, aligning with your research interests in efficient data utilization.

signals.text: PPL-Factory outperforms existing methods, achieving a 0.9 accuracy increase on GSM8K and 4.8 on MATH using only 10% of the training data.

Perplexity scores are computed using negative log-likelihood (NLL), providing a model-aware measure of sample difficulty tailored for both language modeling and reasoning tasks.

deep_dive.overview: The research addresses the inefficiencies in data selection for fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) by introducing PPL-Factory, a framework that integrates task-aware perplexity scoring with budget-aware selection criteria. This approach allows for the effective identification of informative training samples, significantly enhancing model performance while minimizing computational costs. The strongest evidence comes from experiments on GSM8K and MATH, where PPL-Factory demonstrated superior performance compared to existing methods, achieving notable accuracy improvements with a fraction of the training data.

methodology.title: Budget-Aware Selection

methodology.title: Data Selection Problem Formulation

mechanism.title: Perplexity-Based Scoring

experiments.title: GSM8K Evaluation

experiments.title: Comparison with Other Methods

papers.title: Rethinking Heterogeneous LLM Merging: A Weighted Model Averaging Perspective
papers.abstract: Can large language models with substantially different parameter spaces be merged by direct weighted averaging, without training or semantic alignment? Existing heterogeneous fusion methods typically introduce distillation, adapters, learned latent spaces, routing, or feature alignment, leaving open whether a simpler recipe can work for genuinely different billion-parameter checkpoints. We revisit this counterintuitive question through training-free dimensional adaptation followed by ratio-controlled interpolation. In union-style merging, we expand the smaller model into the larger parameter space; in intersection-style merging, we truncate the larger model into the smaller parameter space. Across Qwen-family model pairs and benchmarks covering mathematical reasoning, code generation, language understanding, commonsense reasoning, knowledge, and instruction following, deterministic expansion largely preserves the source model function, and small-ratio interpolation can improve over strong source checkpoints by transferring complementary capabilities. However, near-balanced interpolation often collapses, and task-level results reveal a seesaw effect in which gains on some capabilities coexist with regressions on others. These results show that simple parameter averaging, when paired with lightweight dimensional adaptation and carefully controlled ratios, is a surprisingly strong baseline for heterogeneous LLM merging, suggesting that the limits of direct weighted fusion may also bound what more complex heterogeneous merging methods can achieve at scale.

summary.takeaway: Direct weighted averaging of heterogeneous LLMs can be effective without training or semantic alignment.
summary.problem: Existing methods for merging heterogeneous LLMs often require complex machinery and training.
summary.method: The paper proposes a training-free dimensional adaptation followed by ratio-controlled interpolation for merging.
summary.evidence: Union-style merging with small-ratio interpolation shows performance improvements over strong source checkpoints, achieving an average score of 0.5551.
summary.limitations: The study is limited to Qwen-family checkpoints and does not address broader contexts like multilingual or long-context settings.
summary.why_for_you: This research provides insights into efficient LLM merging strategies relevant for scalable model integration.

signals.text: Deterministic dimensional adaptation allows for effective direct weighted averaging across heterogeneous LLMs, preserving source model functions.
Union-style merging expands the smaller model into the larger parameter space, while intersection-style merging truncates the larger model to the smaller space.
Small-ratio interpolation can enhance model capabilities, but near-balanced ratios may lead to performance collapse, indicating a seesaw effect in task-level results.

deep_dive.overview: This research investigates whether large language models with different parameter spaces can be merged through direct weighted averaging without training or semantic alignment. The authors propose a method involving training-free dimensional adaptation followed by controlled interpolation ratios. Their findings indicate that simple parameter averaging, when combined with dimensional adaptation, serves as a strong baseline for heterogeneous LLM merging. Notably, the results demonstrate that while small-ratio interpolation can yield improvements, it also risks performance collapse at near-balanced ratios, highlighting the complexity of merging strategies.

methodology.title: Dimensional Adaptation
methodology.detail: The method involves expanding the smaller model to fit the larger model's parameter space or truncating the larger model to match the smaller model's dimensions, enabling compatibility for merging.

methodology.title: Weighted Averaging
methodology.detail: After dimensional adaptation, the models are merged using a weighted average based on a controlled mixing ratio, which is crucial for maintaining performance.

methodology.title: Union and Intersection Merging
methodology.detail: Union-style merging expands the smaller model, while intersection-style merging truncates the larger model, allowing for different approaches to model integration.

mechanism.title: Ratio Sensitivity

experiments.title: Qwen Model Evaluation
experiments.detail: The experiments evaluate Qwen2.5 and Qwen3 model pairs across various benchmarks, including GSM8K and MATH-500, demonstrating performance improvements in merged models.

experiments.title: Union Merging Results

experiments.title: Intersection Merging Results

findings.title: Seesaw Effect

Demonstrates the effectiveness of direct weighted averaging in model merging.

papers.title: Digital Pantheon: Simulating and Auditing Coalition Formation with LLM Agents
papers.abstract: The formation of political coalitions is a complex negotiation driven by both concrete policy objectives and deep-seated ideological convictions. While Large Language Models (LLMs) open new avenues for computational political science, the neutrality and helpfulness biases instilled by Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) prevent them from sustaining steadfast partisan behaviour. We present a multi-agent framework that reconciles factual grounding with ideological alignment by combining Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG): DPO instils aggressive party-specific personas, while a per-party RAG pipeline keeps each agent bounded to its official manifesto. We operationalize the framework on the 2019 Flemish election, deploying the partisan agents in a hub-and-spoke negotiation arbitrated by a formateur. To make the emergent negotiation interpretable, we introduce a Multi-Layered Information Lineage Topology (MILT) that traces every clause in the final agreement back to its manifesto origin and classifies it into five provenance states, a Coalition Influence Score (CIS) that aggregates these traceable contributions to identify which party shaped the agreement, and a real-world grounding pass that benchmarks each simulated provision against the historically adopted coalition agreement. Across three independent simulations the framework yields a stable winner and ranking (N-VA ahead of CD\&V and Open Vld), and manifesto-anchored lineage reliably predicts real-world materialization whereas hallucinated content does not. The result is a transparent, scalable testbed for the ex-ante exploration of party compatibility and formateur-mediated compromise.

deep_dive.overview: Digital Pantheon addresses the challenge of simulating political coalition formation with LLM agents that must maintain partisan consistency despite RLHF biases toward neutrality. The framework combines Supervised Fine-Tuning and Direct Preference Optimization to embed party-specific ideological commitments at the model parameter level, while Retrieval-Augmented Generation grounds each agent's utterances in its official party manifesto. methodology.title: Supervised Fine-Tuning and Direct Preference Optimization
methodology.detail: SFT and DPO are applied to embed party-specific ideological commitments into the LLM parameters, enabling agents to maintain aggressive partisan personas during negotiation. DPO optimizes model preferences directly from human feedback data to overcome RLHF neutrality biases.

methodology.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
methodology.detail: Each agent is equipped with a per-party RAG pipeline that retrieves relevant manifesto chunks to ground generation, ensuring factual policy alignment and preventing hallucination beyond official party positions.

methodology.title: Multi-Agent Negotiation Protocol
methodology.detail: A hub-and-spoke communication topology is used where partisan agents negotiate under the arbitration of a formateur agent. This structured deliberation protocol is informed by recent work on communication topologies and decision protocols to simulate realistic coalition bargaining.

methodology.title: Explainability Framework: MILT and CIS

papers.title: Show Me How You Reason and I'll Tell You Who You Are: Reasoning Graphs for Robust LLM Authorship Attribution
papers.abstract: Given the current trend to employ large language models (LLMs) in almost any imaginable context, LLM-generated text detection and authorship attribution have become a pressing issue. Prior work has primarily focused on surface-level linguistic features, an approach shown to be susceptible to paraphrasing and other obfuscation techniques. In this paper, we go beyond the linguistic surface, extracting and analysing reasoning structures in LLM-generated texts with the goal of capturing more complex signals of LLM authorship. We propose a graph neural network approach that leverages reasoning graphs extracted by an argument mining pipeline, demonstrating improved robustness and generalisation over a traditional Longformer baseline. Our approach outperforms the baseline by up to 27 percentage points under the obfuscation attacks such as paraphrasing and backtranslation, and 19 percentage points when evaluated on the texts generated by the unseen model versions, simulating real-world conditions in which new LLM versions are continuously released.

summary.takeaway: Reasoning graph-based authorship attribution using graph neural networks significantly improves robustness and generalisation over text-only baselines for LLM-generated texts under obfuscation and unseen model versions.
summary.problem: Existing LLM authorship attribution methods relying on surface-level linguistic features are vulnerable to paraphrasing and fail to generalise across different model versions.
summary.method: The paper proposes a graph neural network approach leveraging reasoning graphs extracted via an argument mining pipeline to capture structural reasoning features for authorship attribution.
summary.evidence: The reasoning graph-based approach outperforms a Longformer baseline by up to 27 percentage points in F1-score under paraphrasing and backtranslation obfuscations and by 19 points when tested on unseen LLM versions.
summary.limitations: The approach does not employ word-level or character-level perturbations, which may limit evaluation of robustness against finer-grained obfuscations.
summary.why_for_you: This method offers a novel, structurally grounded technique to enhance trustworthy LLM authorship attribution, addressing robustness and generalisation challenges critical for reliable AI-generated text identification.

signals.text: The reasoning graph-based fingerprinting approach achieves up to +27% F1-score improvement over text-only baselines under obfuscation attacks such as paraphrasing and backtranslation, demonstrating superior robustness.

The method constructs reasoning graphs from argumentative essays using the oAMF argument mining pipeline and trains graph neural networks (GCN, GAT, Graph Transformer, GPS) to classify LLM authorship.

Paraphrasing via DIPPER and backtranslation through French and Turkish languages introduce lexical and syntactic variation that reduces lexical diversity and essay length, challenging surface-level detection methods.

deep_dive.overview: The paper addresses the challenge of attributing authorship to texts generated by large language models (LLMs), focusing on robustness to obfuscation and generalisation across unseen model versions. Prior methods relying on surface-level linguistic features are vulnerable to paraphrasing and fail to generalise across evolving LLMs. To overcome this, the authors propose a novel approach that extracts reasoning graphs from argumentative essays using an argument mining pipeline, capturing meta-linguistic and pragmatic structures beyond lexical content. These graphs serve as input to various graph neural network architectures, which learn to classify the originating LLM model. The approach is evaluated on a newly created corpus of 2,240 essays from four LLM families and multiple versions, with obfuscation strategies including paraphrasing and backtranslation. Results show substantial improvements in F1-score over a Longformer baseline, with up to 27 percentage points gain under obfuscation and 19 points gain in cross-version generalisation, demonstrating the effectiveness of structural reasoning features for robust authorship attribution.

methodology.title: Reasoning Graph Construction
methodology.detail: Argument mining pipeline (oAMF) extracts argumentative components and relations from essays, representing sentences as nodes with sentence embeddings and edges as argument relations, forming reasoning graphs that capture the text's structural reasoning.

methodology.title: Graph Neural Network Architectures
methodology.detail: Four GNN variants—Graph Convolutional Networks (GCN), Graph Attention Networks (GAT), Graph Transformer, and General Powerful Scalable (GPS) networks—are trained on reasoning graphs to classify LLM authorship, differing in neighborhood aggregation and attention mechanisms.

methodology.title: Node and Edge Encoding
methodology.detail: Nodes are encoded using sentence-transformer embeddings (all-mpnet-base-v2), while edges are processed via argmax or probability distributions over argument relation classes from the ARIR module, enabling relational reasoning in the graph.

methodology.title: Training and Evaluation Setup
methodology.detail: Models are trained and evaluated on the LLM-OWL-AE corpus with two splits: SAME-VERSION (train/test on same model version) and CROSS-VERSION (train/test on different versions), using 200 essays per model for training and 80 for testing, assessing robustness and generalisation.

methodology.title: Authorship Obfuscation Strategies
methodology.detail: Paraphrasing is applied using the DIPPER tool at paragraph level, and backtranslation is performed via French and Turkish using OPUS-MT models, introducing lexical and syntactic variation to test model robustness.

mechanism.title: No Explicit Mechanism or Equations Provided
mechanism.detail: The paper does not provide formal equations or detailed causal mechanisms but relies on the hypothesis that reasoning graph structures capture meta-linguistic features less affected by surface-level obfuscations, enabling robust authorship attribution.

experiments.title: Dataset and Splits
experiments.detail: The LLM-OWL-AE corpus contains 2,240 argumentative essays from four LLM families and two versions each, with train/test splits for SAME-VERSION and CROSS-VERSION evaluation to test robustness and generalisation.

experiments.title: Baseline and Models
experiments.detail: A Longformer-based text-only baseline is compared against four GNN architectures trained on reasoning graphs, evaluating F1-score performance under original, paraphrased, and backtranslated conditions.

experiments.title: Obfuscation Techniques
experiments.detail: Paraphrasing via DIPPER and backtranslation through French and Turkish are applied to test the models' robustness to lexical and syntactic perturbations that preserve semantic meaning but alter surface features.

experiments.title: Cross-Version Generalisation
experiments.detail: Models trained on earlier LLM versions are tested on later versions and vice versa to assess the ability to generalise authorship attribution across evolving model releases.

findings.title: Robustness to Obfuscation
findings.detail: The reasoning graph-based approach improves F1-score by up to 27 percentage points over the Longformer baseline under paraphrasing and backtranslation obfuscations, demonstrating superior robustness.

findings.title: Generalisation Across Versions
findings.detail: When evaluated on unseen LLM versions, the graph-based method outperforms the baseline by 19 percentage points in F1-score, indicating better generalisation to new model releases.

findings.title: Lexical Diversity Impact
findings.detail: Paraphrasing reduces lexical diversity more severely than backtranslation, with MTLD scores dropping by up to 90 points for some models, challenging surface-level detection but less affecting reasoning graph features.

findings.title: GNN Architecture Performance
findings.detail: Among GNNs, architectures combining local message passing with global attention (GPS) and Graph Transformer variants effectively leverage reasoning graphs for authorship classification.

contributions: Creation and public release of a new dataset of LLM-generated argumentative essays across multiple model versions and families with obfuscation strategies for robustness and generalisation evaluation.
Proposal of a novel reasoning graph-based authorship attribution approach combining language and reasoning features via graph neural networks.
Demonstration of significant performance gains in robustness to obfuscation and generalisation across unseen LLM versions compared to text-only baselines.
limitations: The approach excludes word-level and character-level perturbations, limiting evaluation against finer-grained obfuscation attacks.
No explicit formal mechanism or theoretical explanation is provided for why reasoning graphs capture authorship signals more robustly.
Evaluation is limited to argumentative essays, which may not generalise to other text genres or shorter texts.
Computational resource requirements for argument mining and GNN training are non-trivial, potentially limiting scalability.
open_questions: How well does the reasoning graph-based approach perform on non-argumentative or shorter texts generated by LLMs?
Can the method be extended or adapted to resist finer-grained obfuscations such as character-level perturbations or adversarial paraphrasing?
What are the theoretical underpinnings explaining the robustness of reasoning graphs to obfuscation and model version shifts?
How does the approach scale computationally and perform in real-time or large-scale deployment scenarios?
